displayQuote: I remained too much inside my head and ended up losing my mind

meta.title: Who really said "I remained too much inside my head and ended up losing my mind"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to Edgar Allan Poe, but no source has been found: the line is absent from his collected works, and the Poe Museum finds no evidence he said it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I remained too much inside my head and ended up losing my mind'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Poe all over the internet, yet found in none of his works. The Poe Museum says the evidence is lacking. Here is what the record shows.

answer.label: Unproven for Edgar Allan Poe — no known source
answer.sourceLine: Quote sites credit this line to Poe, but none names a story, poem, essay or letter. It does not appear in his collected works. The Poe Museum’s own fact-check says there is “not sufficient evidence” that he said it. Treat it as an unsourced attribution.

source.heading: The source trail

docMeta.dd: Poe Museum, “Did Poe Really Say That?” (Chris Semtner, Sept. 10, 2014)
The Works of Edgar Allan Poe, Raven Edition (Project Gutenberg): no match

source.excerpt: I remained too much inside my head and ended up losing my mind.
trail: The Poe Museum’s fact-check, “Did Poe Really Say That?” by Chris Semtner (Sept. 10, 2014), lists this line as entry 9. Its verdict: “There is not sufficient evidence to say Poe did not say this, however there is not sufficient evidence to say he did.” Poe Museum blog ↗
Wikiquote’s Edgar Allan Poe page, which collects his sourced quotations, does not include this line. Wikiquote: Edgar Allan Poe ↗

A full-text search of Poe’s collected tales, poems and essays found no “inside my head,” no “losing my mind” and no “remained too much.” The search covered the five-volume Raven Edition and the Complete Poetical Works on Project Gutenberg. Those editions do not include his letters. The Works of Edgar Allan Poe, Raven Edition ↗
Poe’s genuine line on the subject comes from a letter to George W. Eveleth dated January 4, 1848: “I became insane, with long intervals of horrible sanity.” Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore ↗
source.excerptNote: This is the popular wording as it circulates. No Poe text, letter or recorded remark containing it has been found, so it cannot be shown in context.

author.name: Edgar Allan Poe
author.heading: About Edgar Allan Poe
author.metaLine: 1809–1849 · American writer, poet, editor & literary critic
author.bio: Edgar Allan Poe (born Boston, January 19, 1809; died Baltimore, October 7, 1849) was an American writer, poet, editor and literary critic. He is best known for tales such as The Tell-Tale Heart and for poems such as The Raven. Because his narrators so often slide into madness, he attracts a lot of unsourced quotes about insanity. This line is one of them: no work of his has been found that contains it.

misattribution.heading: Where the Poe credit comes from
misattribution.intro: The line spreads through quote collections that attach Poe’s name and give no source. It also circulates in translation.

items.why: A Goodreads list shows the line credited to “Edgar Allen Poe” with no title or work linked. Goodreads list ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The Poe Museum’s verdict stands: there is “not sufficient evidence” that Poe said it, and no one has produced a source. Poe Museum ↗

context.heading: Why it sticks to Poe
lead: Many of Poe’s narrators insist they are sane while describing their own unraveling, and he wrote about his own mental state with real candor. A neat line about thinking yourself into madness sounds like Poe, and that is why it attracts his name.

His actual words on the subject are darker and more specific. In a letter of January 4, 1848, he described the period of his wife’s illness this way: “I became insane, with long intervals of horrible sanity.” Read the letter ↗
